info.text: The human face of hydrology: how gauges and water budgets turn rivers and rain into numbers, how floods and droughts arrive when the balance tips, and how dams, canals, and wells engineer the cycle — sometimes faster than it can refill.

clusters.name: Measuring — putting numbers on water
clusters.fact: Hydrology becomes a science when water gets numbers: gauges record how high and how fast, hydrographs and rating curves turn records into data, and the water balance makes inflow, outflow, and storage add up.

termInfo.stream gauge: A fixed instrument at a river cross-section that continuously records the water level, from which flow is computed.
termInfo.water balance: The accounting equation P = Q + ET + ΔS — precipitation equals streamflow plus evapotranspiration plus the change in storage; also called a water budget.
termInfo.discharge: The volume of water passing a cross-section per unit time — how much river there is, measured in m³/s or ft³/s.
termInfo.stage: The height of the water surface above a reference point at the gauge — how high the river sits right now.
termInfo.hydrograph: A plot of discharge or stage over time; its rising limb is the storm's arrival at the gauge.
termInfo.rating curve: The site-specific calibration that converts a gauge's recorded stage into discharge.
termInfo.hyetograph: A plot of rainfall intensity over time — the input side of the storm that a hydrograph answers.

clusters.name: Extremes — too much and too little
clusters.fact: When the balance tips, water makes headlines: channels overflow their banks, sudden downpours outrun the ground, rains fail for growing seasons — and the '100-year flood' puts a number on how often to expect the worst.

termInfo.flood: An overflow of water that submerges usually-dry land — from river channels overtopping their banks to areal flooding of saturated ground.
termInfo.drought: A prolonged precipitation deficit against demand — the too-little extreme, slow to start and slow to end.
termInfo.flash flood: A rapid, localized flood on steep or impermeable ground, where flow can rise from trickle to torrent in minutes.
termInfo.100-year flood: A discharge sized so it has about a 1% chance in any given year — an average recurrence interval, not a schedule.
termInfo.water scarcity: The persistent failure of fresh water to meet demand — physical when the water is short, economic when the infrastructure is.

clusters.name: Managing — engineered water
clusters.fact: Humans reach into the water cycle with structures and strategies: dams store, aqueducts move, canals irrigate, desalination plants conjure fresh water from the sea — and pumping harder than rain refills is how aquifers get drawn down.

termInfo.dam: A barrier that stores a river's flow behind it, trading downstream flooding and sediment for water supply, flood control, and power.
termInfo.irrigation: Deliberate application of water to grow crops — agriculture is the largest human use of fresh water worldwide.
termInfo.aqueduct: A conduit that moves water across the landscape from where it falls to where people want it.
termInfo.desalination: Removing salt from seawater to make fresh water — a rainfall-independent but energy-hungry source.
termInfo.groundwater overdraft: Pumping an aquifer faster than recharge refills it — the water table falls, wells run dry, and land can subside.
termInfo.levee: An embankment raised along a channel to keep floodwater off the land behind it.

bridges.fact: A '100-year flood' is not a once-per-century promise: it is a discharge with an estimated 1% chance in any given year, read from long gauge records — every hazard's risk number comes from frequency analysis of the measurement record.

info.text: Statistical hydrology analyzes records of rainfall and river flow to estimate how often rare events occur; the return period is an average, not a schedule.

bridges.fact: Flood control is engineering's answer to the too-much-water extreme: dams hold the peak back, levees wall the channel in — structures built because the flood keeps coming, and sometimes overwhelmed when it comes bigger.

info.text: Human changes — wetland loss, urban paving, levees that squeeze channels — often increase flood intensity and frequency even as they try to manage it.

lenses.prompt: Two numbers come off the same stream gauge at the same instant: one tells you how high the water sits, the other how much is moving past. Which terms are they?
lenses.explanation: Stage is the water-surface height at the gauge; discharge is the volume per time moving past — the rating curve converts one into the other. The hydrograph and hyetograph are plots over time, not instant readings.

lenses.prompt: Two of the engineered structures exist chiefly to keep floodwater off the land. Which are they?
lenses.explanation: Dams store the flood peak and levees wall the channel in. Aqueducts and desalination serve water supply, not flood defense — and irrigation spreads water rather than stopping it.

lenses.prompt: Which term names the management failure of pumping an aquifer faster than rainfall refills it?
lenses.explanation: Overdraft is the named condition: the water table falls and wells run dry. Irrigation is a use that can cause it, but exceeding the aquifer's yield is overdraft.

entries.reason: Start with the physical system this board measures and manages: where water sits and how it moves.
Continue with the structure beneath the numbers: drainage networks on the surface, aquifers underneath.

learningIntroduction.summary: Water as a measured, contested, and engineered resource.

content.text:
Water is the resource people measure most obsessively and argue about most fiercely. Hydrology turns rivers, rain, and aquifers into numbers — how much, how fast, how often — and those numbers decide when cities flood, when crops fail, and how much a reservoir must hold.

The human half of that science runs on instruments and ambition: gauges and budgets that make water countable, extremes that break the rules of thumb, and engineering that reshapes the cycle itself.
